blocks.html: Have you ever looked down from a tall slide, a hill, or an airplane window? Things look different from up high. You see the tops of things: roofs, treetops and the tops of cars.
A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking down on it from the sky.

blocks.name: gg-birdseye

opts.readme: Move the slider together. Watch the table, the chair and the cup turn into a map.

blocks.cap: Fly up like a bird. The side view turns into a map.

blocks.html: A picture from the side shows the fronts of things, and the things in front hide the things behind them. From above, nothing hides anything else, so you can see where everything is. That is why every map looks down.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A map of Maple Town. You can see where the school, the store and the park are.

blocks.title: What can a map do?
blocks.q: You want to walk to the park in Maple Town. How can the map help?
steps: Find the park on the map: the green square with trees.
Find where you are starting.
Now you can see which way to go.
blocks.a: The map shows where the park is, so you can find the way.

blocks.html: Some children think a map is like a photo of the front of a house. A map shows the top of the house, the roof, because it looks down from above.
For the grown-up. Stand on a chair together and look down at a table. Name what you see: the top of a cup, the top of a book. Then draw it on paper: that drawing is a map.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2: construct maps and other representations of familiar places

blocks.html: A bird flying over your house sees things in a special way. We call it a bird's-eye view: looking straight down from above.

blocks.name: gg-birdseye
blocks.cap: From the side, and from above.

blocks.html: From above, you see only the top of each thing. A table looks like a rectangle. A tree looks like a round green circle.
When you look straight down, the top of a thing is closest to you, so it covers up everything underneath. The legs of a table and the trunk of a tree hide under their tops.

blocks.title: A cup from above
blocks.q: What does a cup look like from above?
steps: From the side, a cup is tall, with a handle.
From above, you look down into it.
You see the round rim and the drink inside, and the handle sticking out.
blocks.a: A circle with a little handle on one side.

blocks.name: gg-birdseye

opts.readme: Tap a picture in the top row, then the picture that shows it from above. Then press Check.

blocks.cap: Match each thing to its top view.

blocks.html: It is easy to pick the picture that looks like the side view. Ask: if I were a bird looking down, which part would I see first? Usually it is the top.

For the grown-up. Put a few things from the kitchen on the floor: a plate, a cup, a bowl. Let your child look down from a chair and trace their outlines on paper. Round things make circles; boxes make rectangles.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2: construct maps and other representations of familiar places

blocks.html: Now let us make a map of a whole room. Imagine the ceiling is gone and you are a bird looking down into a bedroom.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A map of a bedroom. The door is at the bottom and the window is at the top.

blocks.html: A map of a room shows each thing in the right place, but much smaller than the real room.

A real bed would never fit on a piece of paper. So the mapmaker draws everything smaller by the same amount. The bed stays next to the same wall, and the rug stays in the middle, so the map still tells the truth about where things are.

blocks.title: Reading the room map
blocks.q: What is right in front of the door?
steps: Find the door: the curved line at the bottom of the map.
Look just above it, into the room.
There is the rug, in the middle of the room.

blocks.html: Some children think things on a map must be the real size. A map is like a toy model: everything is smaller, but it is all in the same place.
For the grown-up. Draw a map of your child's room together. Start with the walls (a big rectangle), then the door and the window, then the bed. Ask, "Where does the dresser go?"

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2: construct maps and other representations of familiar places

blocks.html: Maps do not have room to draw every brick and every leaf. So mapmakers use symbols: small pictures or shapes that stand for real things.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: Every little picture on this map is a symbol. Can you find a house, a school and a pond?

blocks.html: A symbol is a little picture or shape on a map that stands for a real thing, like a house, a tree, a road or a school.
A tiny tree symbol is quick to draw and easy to see, even when the real forest has thousands of trees. Symbols keep a map simple, so your eyes can find things fast.

blocks.title: Big things, small symbols
blocks.q: On a map, a hospital is a small blue square with an H. Is the real hospital small?
steps: The symbol is small so it fits on the map.
The real hospital is a big building.
The symbol just shows where it is.
blocks.a: No. The real hospital is big; only the symbol is small.

blocks.name: gg-sort

bins: Things you could see on a map

cards.why: You can hear a song, but a map shows places.
A map shows where, not when.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Which things could a map show with a symbol?

blocks.html: A symbol is not a photo. A red road symbol does not mean the road is red, and a little tree does not mean one little tree. The symbol only says what is there.
For the grown-up. Invent symbols together for your street: a square for your house, a circle for a tree, a line for the sidewalk. Children love making up their own.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2: construct maps and other representations of familiar places

blocks.html: How do you know what a symbol means? Look for the box on the map called the map key. It is also called the legend.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: The map key on the right tells what each symbol means.

blocks.html: The map key shows each symbol and tells what it stands for. When you see a symbol you do not know, check the key.

Different mapmakers draw different symbols. One map might use a tent for a campground, and another might use a triangle. The key is how the mapmaker tells you which is which, so you never have to guess.

blocks.title: Using the key
blocks.q: On the map above, there is a blue shield with a star. What is it?
steps: Find the blue shield in the map key.
Read the words next to it.
The key says: Police station.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A map of Hill Park. Use the key to find the campground and the picnic area.

blocks.html: Children often guess what a symbol means from how it looks. Guessing can go wrong: on the Hill Park map, the green triangle is a tent for the campground, and the gray one is a mountain. Always check the key first.
For the grown-up. Look at a real map together: a zoo map, a park map or a mall map. Find the key first, then go on a symbol hunt: "Where are the restrooms? Where is the snack bar?"

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2: construct maps and other representations of familiar places

blocks.html: Maps use colors too. Colors help you see things quickly, even from far away.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: A world map: blue water and tan land.

blocks.html: On many maps, blue means water, green means parks, forests or low land, and brown or tan means mountains or dry land. But each map's key tells you for sure.
Blue looks like water and green looks like plants, so these colors are easy to remember. Many mapmakers use them, but not all. A mapmaker can pick any colors, as long as the key explains them.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: On this map, each country of South America has its own color.

blocks.title: Why so many colors?
blocks.q: On the map of South America, Brazil and Peru are different colors. Is the land in Peru really the color on the map?
steps: The real land has deserts, mountains and forests of many colors.
The mapmaker colored each country differently.
That way you can see where one country ends and the next begins.
blocks.a: No. The colors just help you tell the countries apart.

blocks.html: Some children think the colors show the real color of the land. On a map like the one above, the colors only show which country is which. Look at the key, or the map's title, to learn what the colors mean.
For the grown-up. Color a simple map together with crayons: blue for a pond, green for a park, gray for roads. Then make a key in the corner with the same colors.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2: construct maps and other representations of familiar places

blocks.html: You know about symbols, the map key and colors. Now let us meet all the parts that help a map do its job.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A map of Maple Town with a title, a map key, a compass rose and a scale bar.

blocks.html: Most maps have four helpers: the title (what place), the key (what the symbols mean), the compass rose (which way) and the scale bar (how far).

items: Title: the name at the top. It says "Maple Town."
Map key: the box of symbols and their names.
Compass rose: the star with N, E, S and W.
Scale bar: the little ruler at the bottom. Here it shows 2 blocks.

blocks.html: A map is a message from the mapmaker to you. Each part answers one question you might ask: What place is this? What does that little picture mean? Which way is north? How far is it?

blocks.title: Which part helps?
blocks.q: You want to know what the little envelope on the map means. Which part do you use?
steps: The envelope is a symbol.
The part that explains symbols is the map key.
The key says the envelope is the post office.

blocks.html: Children mix up the key and the compass rose. The key explains the pictures. The compass rose explains the directions. Ask: "Am I wondering what, or which way?"

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Tells what place the map shows
Shows how far apart places are

opts.readme: Read each card. Your child taps it, then the part of the map that does that job.

blocks.cap: Match each job to its map part.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Find a real map together (a park, a zoo or a road map) and hunt for all four parts. Some maps leave one out; ask your child which one is missing.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: You already know words like on, under and next to from position words. They work on maps too. Let us use them on the map of a bedroom.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A bedroom seen from above. The window is at the top and the door is at the bottom.

blocks.html: Words like left, right, above, below, next to, between, near and far tell where things are.

blocks.title: Between
blocks.q: On the bedroom map, what is between the bed and the toy box?
steps: Find the bed at the top left.
Find the toy box at the bottom left.
In a line between them is the lamp.

blocks.title: Near and far
blocks.q: Is the rug near the door or far from it?
steps: The door is the curved line at the bottom.
The rug is a little above it, in the middle of the room.

blocks.html: On a map, left and right are the left and right of the page as you look at it. Everyone reading the map sees the same left and right, so the words mean the same thing to everyone.
If a picture shows a person facing you, their right hand is on your left. That trips children up. On a map, always use the page's left and right: hold up your own left hand and look.
For the grown-up. Play "I spy" with the bedroom map: "I spy something to the right of the chair." Then switch, and let your child give the clues.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: Left and right change when you turn around. Mapmakers needed direction words that never change. These are the four cardinal directions.

blocks.name: gg-compass
blocks.cap: A house in the middle. The school is north, the pond is east, the store is south and the farm is west.

blocks.html: The four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west. On most maps, north is at the top, south at the bottom, east on the right and west on the left.
North always points toward the North Pole, at the top of the world. It stays the same no matter which way you face. So "the school is north of the house" is true for everyone, wherever they stand.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: On the map above, which way is the farm from the house?
steps: North is at the top of the map.
The farm is on the left side.
Left on this map is west.

blocks.html: Some children think north means "up in the sky" or "straight ahead." North is a direction across the ground, toward the North Pole. We only draw it at the top of the page.

items: North and south are opposites.
East and west are opposites.
Face north: east is on your right, west on your left, and south is behind you.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Find north at home (a phone compass works) and stick a paper "N" on that wall. Then label E, S and W. Ask, "Which wall is the window on?"

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: How do you know which way is north on a map? Look for a little star-shaped drawing. It is called a compass rose.

blocks.name: gg-compass
blocks.cap: A compass rose with the words North, East, South and West.

blocks.html: A compass rose shows the directions on a map. Going around like the hands of a clock from the top, they are north, east, south, west.
Most maps put north at the top, but not all. A map of a trail might be turned to fit the page. The compass rose tells you for sure where north is, so you can find the other directions from it.

blocks.title: A saying to remember
blocks.q: How can you remember the order N, E, S, W?
steps: Start at the top: N.
Go around like a clock: E, then S, then W.
Say: Never Eat Soggy Waffles.
blocks.a: Never Eat Soggy Waffles: north, east, south, west.

blocks.name: gg-compass

opts.readme: Point to the question mark. Say the saying together and count around from N.

blocks.cap: Which direction hides under the question mark?

blocks.html: East and west are easy to swap. Start at N and go around the way a clock's hands turn: the very next one is E, on the right. West is on the left. "We" is on the left, like the "W" in "West."
For the grown-up. Draw a big compass rose on the sidewalk with chalk. Your child stands in the middle and jumps to the direction you call out.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: Now you can use the compass rose to take a walk on a map. One square of the town is one block.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: The walker starts at the house. The line shows 2 blocks south, then 2 blocks east.

blocks.html: To follow directions, do one step at a time: go the number of blocks in the first direction, stop, then go the next number of blocks in the next direction.

blocks.title: A walk in Maple Town
blocks.q: Start at the house in the top left corner. Go 2 blocks south, then 2 blocks east. Where are you?
steps: South is down. Move down 2 squares: you reach the store.
East is right. Move right 2 squares.
You are at the library.

blocks.html: Directions are like a recipe: do the steps in order. Because north, south, east and west never change, two people who follow the same steps from the same place end up in the same spot.
Two common slips: counting the square you start on as "one" (it is zero; you have not walked yet), and turning the wrong way after the first step. Point to the compass rose before each turn.

blocks.name: gg-town

opts.readme: Give your child directions, like "2 blocks north, then 1 block east," and let them press the buttons.

blocks.cap: Take a walk: press North, South, East or West.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Play "robot" in the yard: you give directions like "3 steps north, 2 steps east," and your child walks them out.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: What if a place is not exactly north and not exactly east, but in between? We use the in-between directions.

blocks.name: gg-compass
blocks.cap: A compass rose with eight points: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

blocks.html: The four in-between directions are northeast (NE), southeast (SE), southwest (SW) and northwest (NW). Each one is halfway between two cardinal directions.
Four directions leave big gaps. Eight directions point more exactly, so you can say where things are without long explanations. Sailors and pilots use even more.

blocks.name: gg-compass
blocks.cap: Places all around a house, in eight directions.

blocks.title: Name the corner
blocks.q: In the picture above, which way is the park from the house?
steps: The park is up and to the right.
Up is north and right is east.
Put them together, north first: northeast.

blocks.html: Children sometimes say "eastnorth" or "westsouth." In-between directions always start with north or south: northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest.
For the grown-up. Stand in the middle of a room facing north. Point to the corners together and name them: "That corner is northeast."

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: You do not always have a map or a compass. But on a sunny day, the Sun can help you find your directions.

blocks.name: gg-compass
blocks.cap: In the morning, the Sun rises in the east.

blocks.html: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. So the morning Sun is in the eastern sky, and the evening Sun is in the western sky.

blocks.name: gg-compass
blocks.cap: In the evening, the Sun sets in the west.

blocks.html: Earth spins like a top, the same way every day. As your side of Earth turns toward the Sun, the Sun seems to come up on the east side of the sky. As it turns away, the Sun seems to go down on the west side.

blocks.title: Morning walk
blocks.q: In the morning you walk toward the rising Sun. Which way are you walking?
steps: The Sun rises in the east.
You are walking toward it.

blocks.html: Some children think the Sun is always straight overhead or always in the south. It moves across the sky during the day. In most of the United States it rises in the eastern sky, passes across the southern sky at midday, and sets in the western sky. It rises exactly east only around the first days of spring and fall.
For the grown-up. Notice where the Sun comes up from a window at home. Mark that window "East." Never look straight at the Sun; point to it instead.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
Grokipedia, "Equinox" (the Sun rises due east and sets due west near the equinoxes)

blocks.html: A compass is a small tool with a needle that turns. Hikers and sailors use it to find their way.

blocks.name: gg-compass

opts.readme: Slide to turn the dial until the N lines up with the red needle.

blocks.cap: A compass. The red needle points north. Turn the dial to line up the N.

blocks.html: A compass needle always swings to point north. Turn the compass until the N lines up with the needle. Then every letter on the dial points the right way.
The needle is a tiny magnet. Earth acts like a giant magnet too, and it pulls the needle so that one end points north. That is why the needle swings back, no matter how you turn.

blocks.title: Finding west
blocks.q: The needle points at a big tree. Which way is west?
steps: The needle points north, so the tree is north.
Face the tree. West is on your left.

blocks.html: Some children think the needle points the way they are walking. It does not: it always points north. First line up the N with the needle, then read the direction you want.

For the grown-up. A phone compass app works for practice. Older children may like to know that a compass points to magnetic north, which in most places is close to, but not exactly, true north. Magnets and some metal things can pull the needle off, so hold it away from them.

sources.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, "Magnetic declination" (compasses point toward magnetic north)

blocks.html: Some maps have lines that make squares, like a checkerboard. This is called a grid. It helps us say exactly where something is.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A grid map of Maple Town. Letters run across the top; numbers run down the side. Square B4 is colored.

blocks.html: On a grid map, every square has a name: a letter from the top and a number from the side, like B4.

blocks.title: Name the colored square
blocks.q: What is the name of the colored square?
steps: Go straight up from the square to the top edge. The letter is B.
Go straight across to the side edge. The number is 4.
Letter first, then number.

blocks.html: One letter and one number are enough to point to one square, and only one. It is quicker than saying "the third row, near the middle, kind of on the left."
Children read the number first, or count from the wrong corner. Always say the letter first, and read the letters and numbers printed on the edges instead of counting.

blocks.name: gg-town

opts.readme: Ask your child to tap square C3 and press Check.

blocks.cap: Find square C3.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Play a game of "battleship" on graph paper: hide a sticker in a square and give the square's name.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: You can name a square on a grid. Now turn it around: find a place on the map, then name its square.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: River Town on a grid, with a map key.

blocks.html: To name a place's square: find the place, go straight up to read its letter, then straight across to read its number.

blocks.title: Where is the library?
blocks.q: In River Town, in which square is the library?
steps: Use the key: the library is the building with an open book.
Straight up from it is the letter A.
Straight across is the number 4.

blocks.title: Where is the hospital?
blocks.q: In which square is the hospital?
steps: The hospital is the square with an H.
Up: F. Across: 4.

blocks.html: Grid squares let people find places fast. Many city maps and atlases have an index that lists places with their squares, like "Library ... A4."
It is easy to slip one square over and say A3 or B4. Run your finger in a straight line from the place to the edge, and read the label exactly where your finger lands.
For the grown-up. Older road atlases and many zoo or theme-park maps have a grid index. Look one up together and race to find a place.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: A route is the way you travel from one place to another. You can trace a route on a map with your finger.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: A route from the house to the school: 3 blocks east.

blocks.html: To measure a route on a town map, count the blocks you walk. The route with fewer blocks is shorter.

blocks.title: Two routes to the library
blocks.q: From the house at the top left, Route 1 goes 2 blocks south, then 2 blocks east. Route 2 goes 1 block east, 2 blocks south, then 1 block east. Which is shorter?
steps: Route 1: 2 + 2 = 4 blocks.
Route 2: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 blocks.
They are the same length. Either route works.

blocks.html: In a town you can only walk on streets and paths. You cannot walk through a building or a fence. So the way that looks straightest on the map is not always a way you can go; counting blocks along the streets tells the truth.
Children draw a straight line right through houses and parks, or count the starting square. Follow the streets, and start counting at the first block you walk.

blocks.name: gg-town

opts.readme: Walk from the house to the playground. Count the blocks out loud. Try to find a shorter way.

blocks.cap: Walk your own route.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. On your next walk, choose two ways home and count the blocks of each. Which is shorter?

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section
C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: A map is much smaller than the real place. So how can a map tell you how far something is? It uses a scale bar.

blocks.name: gg-town
blocks.cap: The scale bar says one square is 10 miles.

blocks.html: A scale bar shows how far a length on the map is in real life. Count the lengths, then use the scale to find the real distance.

blocks.title: From the farm to the school
blocks.q: The farm and the school are 4 squares apart. One square is 10 miles. How far is it?
steps: Count the squares: 4.
Skip-count by 10 for each square: 10, 20, 30, 40.

blocks.html: The mapmaker shrinks everything by the same amount. If one square stands for 10 miles everywhere on the map, then 4 squares must stand for 4 tens: 40 miles. That is why the same skip-counting from counting by 5s, 10s and 100s works.

Places that look close are not always close. On a map of your town, one finger-width might be a few blocks. On a map of the whole country, the same finger-width might be hundreds of miles. Always check the scale bar.
For the grown-up. Compare a map of your town with a map of your state. Put a finger on each. Ask, "Is my finger the same distance on both maps?"

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: How does a letter find its way to your home? Its envelope carries your address. Here is a made-up one:

12 Maple Street
Maple Town, Ohio 54321
An address tells exactly where a home is: the house number, the street, the town or city, the state and the ZIP code.

blocks.name: gg-nested
blocks.cap: Each part of the address is a smaller place inside the one before.

blocks.html: Each part narrows the search. The state picks one part of the country. The town picks one place in that state. The street picks one road in the town. The house number picks one home on that street. The ZIP code is a number that helps the mail carriers sort letters quickly.

blocks.title: Reading the address
blocks.q: In the address above, which part is the street?
steps: The first line has a number and a street name.
The number, 12, is the house number.
The words after it are the street.

blocks.html: Children often say only their street or only their town. That is not enough: many towns have a Maple Street, and many states have a town with the same name. All the parts together point to one home.
For the grown-up. Help your child learn your own address. Practice saying it in order, and write it on an envelope together. (Teach it as something to share with trusted grown-ups.)

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: Your home is inside a neighborhood. That neighborhood is inside a town or city. Places fit inside bigger places, like nesting cups.

blocks.name: gg-nested
blocks.cap: Earth holds North America, which holds the United States, which holds a state, a town, a neighborhood and a home.

blocks.html: Your home is in a neighborhood, in a town or city, in a state, in a country (the United States), on a continent (North America), on the planet Earth.
Each bigger place holds many of the smaller ones. One town has many neighborhoods. One state has many towns. One country has many states. That is why we say a place is in another place.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The United States (orange) is one country in North America.

blocks.title: Which is bigger?
blocks.q: Which is bigger: a state or a country?
steps: The United States is a country.
It holds 50 states.
So a country is bigger than one of its states.

blocks.html: Children sometimes think a state is bigger than a country, or that a city and a country are the same kind of place. Use the boxes: a city sits inside a state, which sits inside the country.
For the grown-up. Make a set of nesting labels from paper bags or cups: Earth, North America, our country, our state, our town, our street, our home. Stack them together.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are
C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section

blocks.html: People live in many kinds of places. Some live where buildings are tall and close together. Others live where farms stretch as far as you can see.
A city is a big, busy place with many people. A suburb is a town of homes near a city. A rural place has farms, fields and few houses.

items: City: tall buildings, apartments, buses and subways, crowded sidewalks.
Suburb: streets of houses with yards, schools and shopping centers, close to a city.
Rural: farms, barns, open land and woods, with houses far apart.

blocks.html: Many people work in cities, so people live close together there. Suburbs grew up next to cities so families could have more room and still get to the city. Rural places have the land we need for farms, forests and ranches.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.text: Houses with yards near a big city
A quiet street of homes next to the city

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then the kind of place.

blocks.cap: City, suburb or rural?

blocks.title: What kind of place?
blocks.q: Grandpa lives on a farm. His nearest neighbor is a mile away. What kind of place is that?
steps: There is a farm and lots of open land.
Houses are far apart.

blocks.html: Some children call every town a city, or think rural means "very far from everything." Rural just means few people and lots of open land; a small town can be rural too.
For the grown-up. Talk about where you live and where relatives live. Is it a city, a suburb or a rural place? What clues tell you?

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: Our country, the United States, is made of smaller parts called states. There are 50 of them.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The 50 states. Alaska and Hawaii are drawn in boxes at the bottom left.

blocks.html: The United States is one country made of 50 states. Each state has its own shape on the map and its own name.
A country this big is easier to run in parts. Each state has its own leaders, laws and capital city, and all 50 states together make one country.

blocks.title: The two far-away states
blocks.q: Which two states do not touch any of the others?
steps: Alaska is far to the northwest, next to Canada.
Hawaii is a chain of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
The other 48 states all touch at least one other state.

blocks.name: gg-map

opts.readme: Tap any state to see its name. Can your child find your own state?

blocks.cap: Tap a state.

blocks.html: Some children think a state is a separate country, or that their own state is the whole country. Show the map: your state is one shape, and all 50 shapes together make the United States.
For the grown-up. Find your state on the map, then the states next to it. Texas, California and Alaska are good shapes to learn first because they are big.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: Every country and every state has a special city where its government meets. That city is called the capital.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The star shows Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States.

blocks.html: A capital is the city where a country's or a state's government meets. The capital of the United States is Washington, D.C. On maps, capitals are often shown with a star.
People who make a country's laws need a place to meet and work together. The place for Washington, D.C., was chosen as the nation's capital in 1790. It is not part of any state.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The capitals of four states: Austin, Sacramento, Albany and Tallahassee.

blocks.title: Is the biggest city the capital?
blocks.q: Houston is the biggest city in Texas. Is it the capital of Texas?
steps: Look for the star in Texas.
The star is on Austin.
blocks.a: No. The capital of Texas is Austin.

blocks.html: Many children think the biggest city is always the capital. New York City is the biggest city in the United States (about 8.8 million people in the 2020 Census), but the capital is Washington, D.C. In California the capital is Sacramento, not Los Angeles.
For the grown-up. Learn your own state's capital together. If you can, visit the capitol building, where the state's lawmakers meet.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are
U.S. Census Bureau, QuickFacts: New York city (2020 Census population 8,804,190)

blocks.html: The United States has two big neighbors that share its borders: Canada and Mexico.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Canada to the north, the United States in the middle, Mexico to the south.

blocks.html: The United States is on the continent of North America. Canada is to the north and Mexico is to the south.
On a map, north is at the top. Canada is above the United States on the map, so it is north. Mexico is below, so it is south. All three countries are part of the same continent.

blocks.title: Two neighbors
blocks.q: You drive from Texas straight south and cross the border. Which country are you in?
steps: Texas is at the bottom of the United States.
South of Texas is Mexico.

items: Canada is the second-biggest country in the world by area. Its capital is Ottawa.
Mexico's capital is Mexico City.
The Pacific Ocean is to the west; the Atlantic Ocean is to the east.

blocks.html: Children sometimes think Mexico is in South America because it is "down south." Mexico is in North America; South America starts farther south, past the narrow land of Central America.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The three countries on a globe. Drag to turn it.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. If you have family or friends in Canada or Mexico, find their cities on the map. Notice which way you would travel to visit them.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), Geography, D2.Geo.1.K-2 and D2.Geo.2.K-2: maps of familiar places and where places are

blocks.html: Look at a globe and turn it slowly. You will see a lot of blue. Blue is water. The tan and green parts are land.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: From this side, Earth is almost all ocean. Drag to turn the globe.

blocks.html: Earth has land and water. Water covers about 71 out of every 100 parts of Earth's surface, so there is much more water than land.
People live on land, so it is easy to think land is most of the world. But the oceans are huge. From one side of Earth, over the Pacific Ocean, you can see almost nothing but water.

blocks.title: More land or more water?
blocks.q: If you could put a sticker anywhere on Earth without looking, would it more likely land on water or on land?
steps: About 71 out of every 100 parts of Earth's surface are water.
That is about 7 out of 10.
blocks.a: On water, most of the time.

blocks.name: gg-sort

opts.readme: Read each card. Is it land or water?

blocks.cap: Sort land and water.

blocks.html: Children often guess there is more land, because we live on it. Show a globe from the Pacific side: almost all blue.
For the grown-up. Play the globe game: spin a globe (or a beach-ball globe), stop it with a finger, and count how often the finger lands on water. Most of the time it will.

sources.name: USGS Water Science School, "The distribution of water on, in, and above the Earth" (about 71 percent of Earth's surface is water; the oceans hold about 96.5 percent of its water)
NOAA Ocean Service, "How many oceans are there?" (one global ocean; the Southern Ocean as the fifth)

blocks.html: Land is not flat everywhere. Some land goes up high, and some dips down low. These shapes of the land are called landforms.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: A mountain, a hill and a valley with a river.

blocks.html: A mountain is very high land with steep sides. A hill is lower and rounder. A valley is the low land between hills or mountains.

Rain and melting snow run down the sides of mountains and hills. The water gathers in the low land between them, so a river often flows along a valley's bottom, and over a very long time the river can make the valley deeper.

blocks.title: The highest mountain
blocks.q: What is the highest mountain on Earth?
steps: Mount Everest is in Asia, in the Himalaya mountains.
Its top is about 29,000 feet (8,849 meters) above the sea.

blocks.html: Children call any bump a mountain, or think a valley is a river. A valley is the land; the river is the water that runs through it.

blocks.name: gg-landforms

opts.readme: Tap the mountain, the hill and the valley. Each tap tells what it is.

blocks.cap: Tap any part of the picture to learn its name.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Make landforms with a blanket or play dough: bunch it up high for a mountain, low and round for a hill, and leave a dip between for a valley.
Some land is flat. But flat land can be low, or it can be high up. The two kinds have different names.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: A low plain, a high plateau with a canyon, and mountains.

blocks.html: A plain is wide, flat, low land. A plateau is flat land that is high up, with steep sides, like a giant tabletop.

A plateau is flat on top, like a plain, but it rises high above the land around it. Rivers can cut deep, steep-sided valleys called canyons into a plateau. The Grand Canyon is cut into the Colorado Plateau.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains and the Colorado Plateau.

blocks.title: Plain or plateau?
blocks.q: A wide, flat land with farms stretches for miles, low and level. Is it a plain or a plateau?
steps: It is flat.
It is low, not raised up with steep sides.

blocks.html: Children think all flat land is a plain. Check the height: a plateau is flat too, but high above the land around it.
For the grown-up. Put a book on the table and a sheet of paper beside it. The paper is a plain (flat and low); the book is a plateau (flat on top, with steep sides).
Where land meets water, it makes all sorts of shapes. Two shapes are easy to mix up: islands and peninsulas.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: An island and a peninsula on a coast.

blocks.html: An island is land with water all around it. A peninsula is land with water on three sides that joins bigger land on one side.

You could walk onto a peninsula from the mainland without getting wet, because it is joined on one side. To reach an island you need a boat, a bridge or an airplane, because water goes all the way around.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Florida is a peninsula: water on three sides.

blocks.title: Two real places
blocks.q: Greenland has water all around it. Florida has water on three sides. Which is the island?
steps: Water all around means an island.
Water on three sides means a peninsula.
blocks.a: Greenland is an island (the biggest island in the world). Florida is a peninsula.

blocks.html: A peninsula can look like an island at first glance. Trace the coast with your finger. If you can go all the way around without crossing land, it is an island. If your finger hits the mainland, it is a peninsula.
For the grown-up. At bath time or in a sandbox, make an island (a pile with water all around) and then a peninsula (a strip still joined to the "mainland").
Water comes in different shapes and sizes too. Three of the most important are oceans, lakes and rivers.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: The ocean, a lake and a river.

blocks.html: An ocean is a huge body of salt water. A lake is a body of water with land all around it. A river is water flowing across the land in a long channel.
Rivers carry rain and melted snow downhill. Some flow into lakes, and many end in the ocean. The oceans are salty, but most lakes and rivers are fresh water, the kind people and animals drink.

blocks.title: A very big lake
blocks.q: Are all lakes small?
steps: Some lakes are tiny ponds.
Lake Superior, one of the Great Lakes, is so big you cannot see across it.

blocks.name: gg-sort

opts.readme: Read each card. Is it salty or fresh?

blocks.cap: Salty or fresh?

blocks.html: Children may think a lake and an ocean are the same, or that all water is salty. Oceans are salty and connected to each other. A lake has land all around it, and most lakes are fresh. A few, like the Great Salt Lake, are salty.
For the grown-up. Find a lake and a river near you on a map. Which way does the river flow? Where does it end?

sources.name: USGS Water Science School, "The distribution of water on, in, and above the Earth" (about 71 percent of Earth's surface is water; the oceans hold about 96.5 percent of its water)

blocks.html: A river takes a long trip. Let us follow it from start to end.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: A river from its source in the hills to its mouth at the sea.

blocks.html: A river starts at its source, flows downhill, gets more water from smaller rivers called tributaries, and ends at its mouth, where it flows into a lake, a sea or the ocean.

Water always runs downhill. A river begins up high, at a spring or melting snow, and follows the lowest path down. Mud and sand it carries can pile up at the mouth and build new flat land called a delta.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Nile River in Africa flows north, to the Mediterranean Sea.

blocks.title: Which way does it flow?
blocks.q: Does every river flow south, toward the bottom of the map?
steps: Rivers flow downhill, wherever downhill is.
The Mississippi flows south. The Nile flows north.
blocks.a: No. Rivers can flow in any direction.

blocks.html: Many children think rivers flow "down" the map, toward the south. On a map, "down" just means south. Rivers flow downhill on the land, which can be any direction.
For the grown-up. After a rain, watch water run along the curb or down the driveway. Find where it "starts" and where it "ends": its source and its mouth.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Nile" (flows north to the Mediterranean Sea)

blocks.html: The coast is where the land meets the sea. Coasts are not straight lines; they curve in and out.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: A coast with a bay and a cape.

blocks.html: A bay is part of the sea that curves into the land. A gulf is a very large bay. A cape is a point of land that sticks out into the water.
Land around a bay blocks some of the wind and waves, so the water is often calmer. That is why many towns and harbors are built on bays: boats can stay safe there.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Hudson Bay is a huge bay in Canada.

blocks.title: Bay or lake?
blocks.q: Hudson Bay has land on most sides, but it opens to the ocean in the north. Is it a bay or a lake?
steps: A lake has land all around it.
Hudson Bay opens to the sea.

blocks.html: Children often call a bay a lake. Look for the opening: a bay always opens to the sea on one side. A lake is closed in by land.
For the grown-up. Names do not always follow the rule: some very big waters are called bays and some smaller ones gulfs. Look at a map of a coast you have visited and find a bay, a cape and a beach.
Here is a fun trick. Some land shapes have a water "twin": the same shape, with land and water switched.

blocks.name: gg-landforms
blocks.cap: Three pairs: island and lake, peninsula and bay, isthmus and strait.

blocks.html: Opposite pairs: an island (land in water) and a lake (water in land); a peninsula and a bay; an isthmus (a thin strip of land joining two lands) and a strait (a thin strip of water joining two seas).
Swap the colors in your head. Make the blue land and the land blue: an island turns into a lake, a peninsula into a bay, and an isthmus into a strait.

blocks.title: Two real pairs
blocks.q: The Isthmus of Panama joins North and South America. The Strait of Gibraltar joins the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. Which one is land?
steps: An isthmus is a thin strip of land.
A strait is a thin strip of water.
blocks.a: The Isthmus of Panama is land.

blocks.html: The pairs are easy to mix up. Ask one question: "Is the thin part land or water?" Land: isthmus. Water: strait.

blocks.name: gg-landforms

opts.readme: Ask your child to tap each water twin, then press Check.

blocks.cap: Find the water twins.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Draw an island on paper and color the water blue. Then draw the same shape colored blue with land around it: a lake. Do the same with a peninsula and a bay.
Land can also be described by what covers it: very little, lots of trees, or lots of grass.

blocks.name: gg-biome
blocks.cap: A desert, a grassland and a forest.

blocks.html: A desert gets very little rain. A forest is covered with trees. A grassland is wide open land covered with grass, with few trees.

Plants need water. Where lots of rain falls, trees can grow into forests. Where less rain falls, grass grows better than trees. Where almost no rain falls, only tough plants like cactuses can live: that is a desert.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Three deserts: the Sahara (hot), the Gobi (cold winters) and the Atacama (one of the driest places).

blocks.title: A cold desert
blocks.q: Antarctica is covered with ice and snow. Can it be a desert?
steps: A desert is a place with very little rain or snow each year.
Very little new snow falls in most of Antarctica.
blocks.a: Yes. It is the biggest desert on Earth.

blocks.html: Children picture every desert as hot and sandy. A desert is about how little rain or snow falls, not about heat or sand. Some deserts are rocky, and some are cold.
For the grown-up. Look at photos of deserts, forests and grasslands together. Ask, "Does it rain a lot here or a little? How can you tell?"
Earth is round, like a ball. The best way to show the whole Earth is with a round model of it, called a globe.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: A globe. Drag it, or use the arrow keys, to turn it.

blocks.html: A globe is a small, round model of Earth. It shows land and water in their true shapes and sizes.
Earth is round, so a round model can copy it without stretching anything. Every country, ocean and island keeps its true shape on a globe, just much smaller.

blocks.title: Turning the globe
blocks.q: Can you see all of Earth at once on a globe?
steps: A globe is round, like a ball.
You can only see the side that faces you.
Turn it to see the other side.
blocks.a: No. You see half at a time, and turn it to see the rest.

items: Blue shows the oceans.
The North Pole is at the top; the South Pole is at the bottom.
Many globes spin on a tilted stand, because Earth's spin is tilted too.

blocks.html: Children who mostly see flat maps may think Earth is flat. A flat map is a drawing of a round Earth on flat paper. The globe is the truer model.
For the grown-up. If you have a globe or a beach-ball globe, find your country together, then spin it to find the other side of the world.

sources.name: C. C. Long, Home Geography for Primary Grades (1894), lessons on direction and maps, in the Teddy Rook Book Homeschool section

blocks.html: A globe is true, but you cannot fold it into your pocket. A flat map is handy, but it has a secret: it has to stretch some places.

blocks.name: gg-projection
blocks.cap: Two flat maps. On the first, Greenland looks as big as Africa. On the second, you can see Africa is much bigger.

blocks.html: A flat map is easy to carry and shows the whole world at once, but it stretches some places. A globe shows true shapes and sizes, but you see only one side at a time.
Try to flatten an orange peel: it tears or stretches. A round Earth cannot lie flat without changing something. Many flat maps stretch the places near the North and South Poles the most.

blocks.title: Greenland and Africa
blocks.q: On some flat maps, Greenland looks as big as Africa. Which is really bigger?
steps: Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometers.
Africa covers about 30.4 million square kilometers.

blocks.name: gg-projection

opts.readme: Drag Greenland's true-size outline down toward Africa and watch it shrink.

blocks.cap: Drag Greenland's true size around the map.

blocks.html: Many people believe Greenland is as big as Africa, because they saw it that way on a flat map. Check sizes on a globe.
For the grown-up. Peel an orange in one piece and try to press the peel flat. Talk about how a map has the same problem.
The biggest pieces of land on Earth are called continents. Most people learn that there are seven.

blocks.name: gg-map

catNames: Russia (part in Europe, part in Asia)

blocks.cap: The seven continents. Russia has its own color because part of it is in Europe and part is in Asia. Antarctica is the white land at the bottom.

blocks.html: The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.

A continent is a huge area of land that holds many countries (Antarctica has none). Some places count the continents a little differently, for example by joining North and South America into one. In the United States, most schools count seven.

blocks.title: Country or continent?
blocks.q: Is Africa a country?
steps: Africa is one of the seven continents.
It holds many countries: 54 that are members of the United Nations.
blocks.a: No. Africa is a continent with more than 50 countries.

blocks.name: gg-sort

cards.why: France is a country in Europe.
Texas is a state in the United States.
Canada is a country in North America.

opts.readme: Read each card. Is it a continent?

blocks.cap: Continent or not?

blocks.html: Children often call Africa or Asia a country. A continent is much bigger: it holds many countries. Remember: there are only seven continents.
For the grown-up. Sing or chant the seven continents together. Many children learn them fastest with a tune.
Now let us find each of the seven continents by its shape and its place on the map.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The seven continents on a world map.

blocks.html: Asia is the biggest. Australia is the smallest. Antarctica is at the bottom, covered in ice. North America is above South America. Europe is above Africa.

items: North America and South America are on the left, joined by a thin strip of land.
Europe and Asia share one huge piece of land; Europe is the smaller western part.
Africa is in the middle, below Europe.
Australia is at the bottom right.

blocks.html: Where a continent sits helps you find it: the Americas on the left side of most world maps, Africa in the middle, Asia on the right, Antarctica along the bottom.

blocks.title: Two Americas
blocks.q: Which America is on top?
steps: North is at the top of the map.
So North America is on top, and South America is below it.

blocks.html: Children mix up North and South America, and Europe and Asia, because each pair is joined. North is up. Europe is the smaller part to the west (left); Asia is the giant part to the east.

blocks.name: gg-globe

opts.readme: Turn the globe and name each continent as it comes around.

blocks.cap: Turn the globe to find all seven.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Cut the seven continents out of an old map or a coloring page and put them together like a puzzle.
Between the continents are the oceans. Most people name five of them.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The five oceans and the seven continents.

blocks.html: The five oceans are the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Arctic and the Southern. The Pacific is the biggest, and the Arctic is the smallest.

All the oceans are connected; together they make one big world ocean. People gave its parts names to help find places. The Southern Ocean, all around Antarctica, is the newest name on many maps; the United States recognizes it as the fifth ocean.

items: Pacific: between Asia and Australia and the Americas.
Atlantic: between the Americas and Europe and Africa.
Indian: south of Asia, between Africa and Australia.
Arctic: around the North Pole.
Southern: all around Antarctica.

blocks.title: Which ocean?
blocks.q: You sail from the United States to Europe. Which ocean do you cross?
steps: The United States is in North America, on the left of the map.
Europe is across the water to the right.
That water is the Atlantic Ocean.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica.

blocks.html: Children may think the oceans are separate pools. A ship could sail from one ocean into the next without ever touching land.
For the grown-up. Trace a path with your finger from ocean to ocean on a globe without crossing land.

sources.name: NOAA Ocean Service, "How many oceans are there?" (one global ocean; the Southern Ocean as the fifth)

blocks.html: Many animals live wild on only one continent. Knowing where they live helps you remember the continents.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Some animals and their wild homes.

blocks.html: Kangaroos and koalas live wild in Australia. Giraffes and zebras live wild in Africa. Emperor penguins live on and around Antarctica. Giant pandas live wild in Asia.

items: North America: American bison, bald eagle.
South America: Amazon river dolphin, Andean condor.
Europe: Iberian lynx (Spain and Portugal), Alpine ibex.
Asia: giant panda (China), tiger, orangutan.

blocks.html: Animals live where their food, weather and homes are right for them, and oceans keep many of them from spreading. That is why kangaroos stayed in Australia.

blocks.title: Zoo or wild?
blocks.q: You saw a giraffe at a zoo in Ohio. On which continent does it live in the wild?
steps: A zoo is not an animal's wild home.
Wild giraffes live in Africa.

blocks.html: Children place an animal where they saw it, in a zoo or a book. Ask: "Where does it live on its own?" A few animals live on more than one continent: wild elephants live in Africa and in Asia, and polar bears live around the Arctic in North America, Europe and Asia.
For the grown-up. Pick a favorite animal and look up together where it lives in the wild. Put a sticker on that continent.
Mapmakers draw some lines on maps that you cannot see on the ground. The most famous one goes around the middle of Earth.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The equator goes around the middle of Earth.

blocks.html: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth, halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole.

Earth spins around an imaginary line through the poles. The equator is the circle exactly halfway between them. Its name comes from "equal": it cuts Earth into two equal halves. It is about 25,000 miles (40,000 kilometers) around.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The equator crosses South America and Africa, and islands of Asia.

blocks.title: Where does it go?
blocks.q: Which two continents does the equator cross in the middle of the map?
steps: Follow the line from left to right.
It crosses South America, then the Atlantic Ocean, then Africa.

blocks.html: Some children think the equator is a real line painted on the ground. It is imaginary. In a few places people have put up signs or a painted line for visitors, but the line itself is just a way to find places.
For the grown-up. Put a rubber band around the middle of a ball. That is the equator. Mark a dot on top for the North Pole and a dot underneath for the South Pole.
At the very top and the very bottom of Earth are two special places: the North Pole and the South Pole.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The North Pole is in the middle of the Arctic Ocean.

blocks.html: The North Pole is the farthest point north, in the Arctic Ocean. The South Pole is the farthest point south, on the continent of Antarctica.

There is no land at the North Pole. It is in the middle of the Arctic Ocean, which is covered by floating sea ice. The South Pole is on land: Antarctica, buried under ice that is more than a mile thick.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The South Pole is on Antarctica.

blocks.title: Who lives where?
blocks.q: Do polar bears and penguins meet at the North Pole?
steps: Polar bears live in the far north, around the Arctic Ocean.
Almost all wild penguins live in the southern half of the world; emperor penguins live around Antarctica.
blocks.a: No. They live at opposite ends of the world.

blocks.html: Children often think the North Pole is on land, or that penguins live there. The North Pole is on ice floating on the ocean, and wild penguins live in the south.
For the grown-up. On a globe, put one finger on the North Pole and one on the South Pole. Every line from pole to pole on the globe meets at your fingers.

sources.name: NOAA NESDIS, "Five things you didn't know about the North Pole" (no land at the North Pole; floating sea ice on the Arctic Ocean)

blocks.html: If you cut a ball in half, each half is a hemisphere. Mapmakers cut Earth in half in two ways.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The Northern Hemisphere is shaded. It is the half north of the equator.

blocks.html: The equator cuts Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. A line from pole to pole cuts it into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.

The east-west cut follows the line from the North Pole to the South Pole through London, England, and the line on the other side of the world. Since there are two different cuts, every place is in two hemispheres at once: one northern or southern, and one eastern or western.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The equator (across) and the lines from pole to pole that split east from west.

blocks.title: Two at once
blocks.q: The United States is north of the equator and west of London's line. Which hemispheres is it in?
steps: North of the equator: the Northern Hemisphere.
West of London's line: the Western Hemisphere.
blocks.a: The Northern and Western Hemispheres. (A few of Alaska's far-off islands cross into the east.)

blocks.html: Children think a place can be in only one hemisphere. Every place is in two: north or south, and east or west. Australia is in the Southern and Eastern Hemispheres.
For the grown-up. Cut an orange in half across the middle (north and south), and another one from top to bottom (east and west). Talk about which half your home is in.
